# LITs with `tags` `mathematical-statistics`

*Topics — What a work is about. Nucleation holds whatever reading the owner files here, whether or not an Anthology of the SOTA topic could also hold it; instruction for ML practice belongs to the anthology (ADR-048). **Mathematical statistics** — the theory of statistical inference read for itself — comparison and sufficiency of experiments (Blackwell, Le Cam deficiency), statistical decision theory, the sufficiency theorems (Fisher–Neyman, Basu, Bahadur) and bounds on estimation. Bayesian modelling is probabilistic-modeling (ADR-031).

| [LIT-781](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-781.md) | Equivalent Comparisons of Experiments | Blackwell (1953), Ann. Math. Statist. 24(2):265–272. Completes the Blackwell order: for finitely many states, one experiment is at least as informative as another for every decision problem exactly when the other is a garbling of it. The easy direction is Blackwell (1951) and the finite converse Sherman and Stein's; this paper re-proves the converse by minimax, extends it to arbitrary outcome spaces by a martingale argument, introduces comparison by k-action problems, and reduces two-state comparison to the type I/type II error trade-off. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-595](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-595.md)); worth reading as the paper in which the comparison of experiments is settled in general: for experiments with finitely many states, being at least as informative in every decision problem (Bohnenblust, Shapley and Sherman's order) and being able to reproduce the other by a stochastic transformation (Blackwell's 1951 sufficiency, later called garbling) are the same order. The finite-outcome converse is Sherman and Stein's, re-proved here by a minimax argument; the extension to arbitrary outcome spaces, by martingale convergence, is new. It adds comparison by k-action problems, and shows that for two states testing problems, and so the type I/type II error curves, decide the order. |

HodgeRank. Pairwise comparisons, aggregated into a weighted edge flow on the graph of alternatives, decompose orthogonally into a gradient flow, the l2-best global ranking found by weighted least squares, and a divergence-free residual. The residual splits into curl (local, triangular inconsistency) and harmonic (global inconsistency) parts. Binary win/loss data enter as averaged signs, and on complete balanced binary data the ranking is Borda's. The decomposition is cardinal: curl-freeness is stronger than transitivity. It is the tool for reading the record's conflict record. |
| [LIT-1523](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1523.md) v3 | Sequential Tests of Statistical Hypotheses | Wald (1945). Introduces the sequential probability ratio test: observations are taken one at a time, the log-likelihood ratio of two simple hypotheses is accumulated, and sampling stops when it leaves an interval whose bounds are set approximately from the desired error probabilities. The paper derives the test's operating characteristic and its expected number of observations, which for given error rates is substantially smaller than the fixed sample a test of the same strength needs, and proves that no test of the same strength needs fewer on average once the overshoot of the bounds is neglected (checked against the reading). | Active — read 2026-10-25 ([NOTE-1165](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1165.md)) in full, from the copy the owner supplied on 2026-10-25, a JSTOR scan of the Annals article (this client had been stopped by Project Euclid's bot check the same day). Worth reading as the source of the sequential probability ratio test: its boundaries follow from the error rates alone, A = (1 − β)/α and B = β/(1 − α) ([THEORY-952](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-952.md)), and its operating characteristic, expected sample size and optimality against every test of the same strength are derived, with savings of about half against the fixed-sample test ([THEORY-951](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-951.md)). Read it knowing that optimality is proved only when the overshoot of the boundaries is neglected, the exact case being a conjecture (footnote 12), that the operating characteristic and sample-size formulas are approximations that need i.i.d. observations, and that the paper never mentions diffusion: the drift-diffusion limit is later work's, and is the case in which these approximations are exact. |

| [LIT-1622](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1622.md) v2 | Beam Sampling for the Infinite Hidden Markov Model | Van Gael, Saatci, Teh & Ghahramani (2008), ICML '08: 1088–1095. For the infinite hidden Markov model (the HDP-HMM), an auxiliary variable u_t ~ Uniform(0, π_{s_{t−1}s_t}) per time step leaves only finitely many trajectories with positive probability, so a whole state sequence can be resampled by dynamic programming without truncation. On synthetic data, a well-log changepoint series and character prediction in Alice in Wonderland, the beam sampler mixes in fewer iterations and is less sensitive to initialization and priors than the Gibbs sampler, at a cost per iteration close to O(TK) in practice. | Active — read 2026-10-27 ([NOTE-1204](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1204.md)) in full, from the authors' own copy of the ICML paper; worth reading for the beam sampler, which adds a uniform slice variable under each transition so that only finitely many state trajectories of the infinite HMM have positive probability, and then samples a whole trajectory exactly by forward filtering, backward sampling ([THEORY-1037](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1037.md)). The infinite factorial HMM's inference is built on it. Read it knowing that its case for faster mixing than Gibbs sampling rests on charts, synthetic data and one changepoint series judged by eye ([THEORY-1044](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1044.md)), and that one of its fixed hyperparameter settings was chosen from the samplers' own results. |
| [LIT-1623](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1623.md) v2 | Infinite Latent Feature Models and the Indian Buffet Process | Griffiths & Ghahramani (2005), NIPS 18. A finite model in which each of K features has prevalence π_k ~ Beta(α/K, 1) and each of N objects holds it with probability π_k has, as K → ∞, a limit on left-ordered equivalence classes of binary matrices; the Indian buffet process, in which customer i takes each earlier dish with probability m_k/i and then Poisson(α/i) new ones, produces the same distribution. It is used as the prior of an infinite binary linear-Gaussian latent feature model, with a Gibbs sampler, on 100 photographs of up to four objects. | Active — read 2026-10-27 ([NOTE-1208](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1208.md)) in full, from the NeurIPS proceedings' own PDF; worth reading as the paper that introduces the Indian buffet process, the limit of a finite beta–Bernoulli feature model taken on left-ordered equivalence classes, and its sequential buffet, which produce the same distribution ([THEORY-1043](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1043.md)). Read it knowing that its eight pages state the limit and defer the technical details to a technical report, that it gives K+ ~ Poisson(αH_N) only through the buffet, with no count for the finite model, and that its one demonstration is a single run on 100 staged photographs, in which three of the four main features code an object's absence. |
| [LIT-1626](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1626.md) v2 | Infinite Sparse Factor Analysis and Infinite Independent Components Analysis | Knowles & Ghahramani (2007), ICA 2007, LNCS 4666: 381–388. Data are modelled as Y = G(Z ⊙ X) + E, with a potentially infinite number of hidden sources X, a binary mask Z drawn from the one- or two-parameter Indian buffet process, and a Gaussian (infinite sparse factor analysis) or Laplacian (infinite ICA) prior on the sources. A Gibbs sampler with Metropolis–Hastings steps for new features recovers a synthetic mask and beats FastICA in Amari error on sparse synthetic data, and finds tissue-specific gene signatures in ovarian cancer microarray data. | Active — read 2026-10-27 ([NOTE-1209](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1209.md)) in full, from the authors' own copy of the ICA 2007 paper; worth reading for infinite sparse factor analysis and infinite ICA, in which an Indian buffet process masks which of unboundedly many sources is active at each data point, the model the infinite factorial HMM's experiments compare against, and for its sampler, whose ratio for a source being on or off shows how far the data can tell an inactive source from an active one at zero ([THEORY-1046](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1046.md)). Read it knowing that its results are boxplots and a Hinton diagram, that its text and figure caption disagree on the synthetic data's size, and that it misstates the one-parameter IBP's total number of features. |
| [LIT-1627](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1627.md) v2 | Stick-breaking Construction for the Indian Buffet Process | Teh, Görür & Ghahramani (2007), AISTATS, PMLR 2: 556–563. In the limit of the IBP's finite model, the feature probabilities in decreasing order are μ_(k) = ∏_{l≤k} ν_l with ν_l ~ Beta(α, 1) independent; the pieces broken off are the Dirichlet process's GEM(α) weights. A slice sampler built on it truncates the representation adaptively and needs no conjugacy; a semi-ordered variant, on synthetic linear-Gaussian data, mixes as fast as the conjugate Gibbs sampler, and it is demonstrated on 1000 MNIST threes. | Active — read 2026-10-27 ([NOTE-1210](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1210.md)) in full, from PMLR's own PDF; worth reading for the stick-breaking construction of the Indian buffet process, in which the feature probabilities in decreasing order are products of independent Beta(α, 1) draws, for its duality with the Dirichlet process's sticks, and for the slice samplers it licenses, which the Markov IBP's inference uses ([THEORY-1041](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1041.md)). Read it knowing that its truncation is described but its error is not computed, that its sampler comparison is reported only as a chart of autocorrelation times, and that its MNIST demonstration is a single run judged by eye. |
